prompt:
Can you help with a 44-year-old high school soccer coach who has three days of sharp retrosternal chest pain that's worse lying down and better leaning forward, starting a week after a cold? ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; troponin is undetectable on two draws; echo shows a trivial pericardial effusion with normal LV function. Temperature is 37.8 C. He has stage 3a CKD (eGFR 50), a duodenal ulcer eight years ago, and hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 40 mg, and urgent care started clarithromycin yesterday for sinusitis. He weighs 84 kg and wants to get back to coaching and his weekend league. What treatment would you start?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Confirm acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis without high-risk features such as fever above 38 C, large effusion, tamponade, myocardial involvement, anticoagulation, or immunosuppression.
Manage him as an outpatient given the absence of high-risk features.
Start colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for about three months.
Stop clarithromycin before starting colchicine because of the dangerous CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein interaction.
If antibiotics are truly needed for sinusitis, substitute a non-interacting agent such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline.
Consider a lower colchicine dose and closer monitoring given his reduced renal function.
Prescribe a short course of anti-inflammatory therapy such as ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily or high-dose aspirin, with a taper, using caution given his CKD and ulcer history.
Co-prescribe a proton pump inhibitor with the NSAID or aspirin given his prior duodenal ulcer.
Check creatinine and potassium within one to two weeks of starting NSAID therapy.
Confirm that prior Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication were completed.
Check CRP at baseline and use it to guide treatment duration and taper.
Taper the NSAID or aspirin only after symptoms resolve and CRP normalizes.
Restrict competitive sports and strenuous exertion until symptoms, CRP, and ECG normalize, typically for at least one to three months for competitive athletes.
Counsel him about muscle pain or weakness because colchicine combined with a statin increases myopathy risk.
Counsel on colchicine gastrointestinal side effects and to stop it and call if severe diarrhea develops.
Schedule follow-up in about one week to assess response.
Repeat echocardiography if symptoms worsen or effusion is suspected to be enlarging.
Advise urgent return for dyspnea, lightheadedness, syncope, or worsening chest pain.
Evaluate for alternative causes such as tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, or malignancy if there is no response within one week.
Continue atorvastatin with myopathy monitoring rather than stopping it.
Explain the risk of recurrence and that colchicine reduces it.
Start colchicine while continuing clarithromycin.
Prescribe prednisone as first-line therapy.
Prescribe high-dose NSAIDs without gastroprotection.
Combine two NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen.
Start therapeutic heparin for the chest pain.
Admit for cardiac catheterization.
Perform pericardiocentesis for the trivial effusion.
Clear him to return to competitive soccer as soon as the pain resolves.
Prescribe colchicine for only one week.
Give a gout-style colchicine loading dose.
Order cardiac MRI routinely despite normal troponin and uncomplicated disease.
Send extensive autoimmune, tuberculosis, and viral serologies routinely at the first episode.
Start empiric antibiotics for bacterial pericarditis.
Use opioids as primary therapy instead of anti-inflammatory treatment.
Continue NSAIDs indefinitely without monitoring renal function.
Stop the NSAID after a fixed five-day course regardless of symptoms and CRP.
Start anakinra or intravenous immunoglobulin for this first uncomplicated episode.
Refer for surgical pericardiectomy.
